passage: Jeevan's history essay came back with the lowest mark he had ever got and a comment that the argument was missing. He was sure he had written one. He did not complain to the class, and he did not sit in silence either. That evening he underlined the paragraph, copied the marking rubric from the school portal and waited by Ms Rashmi's table after class. "Ma'am, may I show you where I think my argument is? I might have misread what the rubric wants." She read the paragraph twice. "Ah. Page three was stuck to page four. I only read half your essay." She corrected the mark and said, "Thank you for asking politely rather than telling me off." Jeevan felt his shoulders drop.

qa.q: What did Jeevan bring to show Ms Rashmi?
qa.a: He brought the underlined paragraph and the marking rubric.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan say he might have misread what the rubric wants?
qa.a: He wanted to raise his concern politely without accusing her, and left room for the possibility that he was the one who was wrong.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do if the teacher had disagreed?
qa.a: He could listen to her reasons, ask how to improve, or take the concern to the coordinator or head through the school's proper channel.

qa.q: How might Ms Rashmi have felt when Jeevan approached her?
qa.a: She was probably relieved that he asked calmly, since she admitted her mistake and thanked him.

grounding: A student raises a concern about marking politely with evidence instead of staying silent or being disrespectful.

passage:
"Santosh Sir, may I talk to you about my project mark?"
"The mark is final, Ayesha. You submitted late."
"I understand, Sir. I just want to show you something." She held out her phone. "The upload page crashed at 11:52. Here's the screenshot of the error, and my email to you at 11:55 with the file attached."
"Hmm."
"Five other students had the same error. Meena and Joel have screenshots too."
"Why didn't you raise it at the time?"
"I did, in the email. I think it went to spam."
"Let me check with the IT office. If this is right, I'll correct all six marks."
"Thank you, Sir. And if the IT office can't confirm it, could we ask the coordinator?"
"Fair. Come by on Friday."

qa.q: At what time did the upload page crash?
What might Ayesha have been feeling when she first asked about her mark?
qa.a: Ayesha probably felt nervous and wronged, but determined to be heard fairly.
She stayed polite, brought evidence like the screenshot and email, named others affected and suggested the coordinator as a proper channel.

qa.q: How does Santosh Sir see the screenshot?
qa.a: Santosh Sir seems to see it as fair evidence that makes him rethink, which is why he agrees to check with the IT office.

grounding: Illustrates a teen raising a concern about an unfair mark politely, with evidence and a proper channel.

passage: I'm Kavitha, and last term I learned this the hard way. Mrs Rao kept picking the same four students for the debate team, even when Ira and I had higher scores in the trials. For a month I said nothing and just sulked. Nothing changed. Then one day I snapped in class: "You only pick your favourites!" The room went silent, and I got sent out. That didn't help either. Ira suggested another way. We collected the trial score sheets, wrote a short, polite letter asking how selection worked, and took it to the English coordinator. Two weeks later the school put up clear selection rules on the notice board. I made the team in the next round. I still cringe about snapping, though.

qa.q: Who kept picking the same four students?
qa.a: Mrs Rao kept picking the same four students for the debate team.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling during the month of saying nothing?
qa.a: Kavitha felt resentful and unfairly treated, sulking because the higher trial scores seemed ignored.

qa.q: Which approach finally worked, and why?
qa.a: Collecting the score sheets and taking a polite letter to the English coordinator used evidence and a proper channel, so the rules became clear.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao have felt when Kavitha snapped in class?
qa.a: Mrs Rao probably felt accused and embarrassed in front of everyone, which made her less open to the complaint.

grounding: Shows a teen learning that silence and disrespect both fail against a seemingly unfair teacher, while evidence and a proper channel work.
